newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Hopefuls line up for NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: Hopefuls line up for NATO membership.

text.p: Hungary, Poland, and the Czech Republic are favourites to become the first of NATO's former communist enemies to achieve full membership of the alliance by a 1999 target date set by President Bill Clinton on Tuesday.
"Those three are virtually a shoo-in now, even Russia unofficially accepts that," said one senior European diplomat.
Functioning democracies, civilian control of the armed forces and market economies are the three basic conditions all applicants must meet.

Budapest, Warsaw and Prague already essentially meet those requirements. The same three also lead the field to win swift membership to the European Union in the most radical change to the continent's security structure in 50 years.

In addition, working closely with the alliance's military, they have made substantial progress bringing their armed forces in line with those of NATO countries -- ranging from teaching English to officers to buying NATO-standard equipment.
NATO sources say the cost of alliance enlargement is currently impossible to estimate as it depends on what these countries are asked to do and by when.

"If they were asked to modernise their air defence systems in line with those of NATO allies, it would cost a fortune, but there is absolutely no need to do that. Many of those things can be tackled after membership," one military expert said.
Hot on the heels of those three countries come Slovakia, Slovenia and Romania.

Romania has won admirers in NATO for the hard work it has put in on restructuring its armed forces along the recommended lines and for the enthusiasm with which it has tackled tasks assigned under the Partnership for Peace programme.
But its economy is weak and many NATO allies feel it is simply not ready to assume fully the responsibilities of membership.
NATO's interim report on enlargement stresses the need for new members to be "providers as well as consumers of security".
Once among the favourites, Slovakia has slipped from grace following a feud between populist Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar and President Michal Kovac.
The United States has criticised Meciar's government for failing to play by democratic rules and for dragging its heels on economic reforms.

Slovenia, the former Yugoslav republic which escaped the worst of the Balkan wars, has emerged in recent months as the most likely outsider. Its economy is booming and its army restructured and firmly under civilian control.
Several allies feel it should be rewarded if for no other reason than as an example to other states in the Balkans.

Bulgaria, another country with a weak economy, has requested closer links with the alliance. Membership remains a long-term goal, but Sofia has shown little interest in pushing its case to be in the first wave.
Lastly come the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia.

The strategic importance to Russia of these former Soviet republics makes them unlikely to gain entry in the foreseeable future to NATO, whose military also stress the impossibility of defending them.
"It is ironic, but those countries that perhaps most need it (NATO's security guarantee) are those most unlikely to get it," said one NATO ambassador.
